inputs.question: In low- and middle-income countries, do programmes meant to improve education for children and young people with disabilities work, and which kinds work best?
inputs.scope:
Covers: Interventions meant to improve educational access, participation or learning outcomes for children and young people with disabilities (any impairment type) in low- and middle-income countries. Settings include mainstream, special and community programmes. The question covers whether such programmes have measurable effects on enrolment, attendance, retention, progression and learning, and how different types of intervention compare.
Out of scope:
- Education programmes for disabled children in high-income countries (School systems, resources and the evidence base differ too much to transfer findings to low- and middle-income settings.)
- Whether inclusive education is a human right or a legal obligation (e.g., under UNCRPD Article 24) (This is a normative and legal question, not an empirical question about effectiveness.)
- Health or rehabilitation outcomes of disability programmes (e.g., motor function, hearing improvement) when no education outcome is measured (The question concerns educational outcomes. Clinical effects alone do not show whether schooling improved.)
- The prevalence of disability among out-of-school children and the size of the education gap (Describing the gap is different from testing whether interventions close it.)
- The cost-effectiveness and financing of disability-inclusive education (This needs cost data and economic modelling beyond effectiveness evidence. It is noted only where reviews report it.)
